title: The Uncomfortable Reason Personality Assessments Are So Popular in Leadership Development
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note offers a structural critique of the leadership development industry: personality assessments dominate organizational training programs not primarily because they are the most effective tools for developing leaders, but because assessment certifications give HR and talent development professionals informational power over the senior leaders they serve. The article grants that self-awareness is a genuine prerequisite for leadership growth, but argues that self-awareness is only half of development -- without learning precisely what to do differently, knowing one's personality type does not change behavior. The real critique is institutional: the professionals who decide what leadership programs organizations invest in are often the same professionals whose status depends on running assessment-based programs. Becoming certified to administer Myers-Briggs, DISC, Hogan, Enneagram, StrengthsFinder, or Big Five gives practitioners a brief window where they know something about senior leaders that those leaders do not know about themselves -- a reversal of the normal power dynamic that feeds professional ego. Until senior leaders demand programs that balance personality awareness with concrete behavioral skill-building, the incentive structure will continue to produce leaders who don't develop as they should.
points: Self-awareness is only half of leadership development: without learning precisely what to do differently, even deep insight into one's personality will not change leadership effectiveness.

Assessment certifications confer informational power over senior leaders that reverses the normal organizational hierarchy, giving practitioners a brief window where they know something about executives that the executives don't know about themselves.

The professionals who recommend and decide leadership program investments are often the same professionals whose value and status depend on personality assessment programs remaining dominant -- a structural conflict of interest that distorts what organizations buy.

The consequence is millions of leaders who stop developing because the programs they receive are designed more around their providers' professional incentives than around what would actually make them more effective.
The corrective requires senior leaders themselves to insist on programs that balance personality assessment with explicit best practices and behavioral skill development.
quotes: At best, self-awareness is only half of the development process, and tools that provide a deeper understanding of people are not, on their own, enough to make leaders better. Without learning precisely what to do differently, leaders don't change their behavior.

Human resources professionals, executive coaches, and other talent experts can easily become 'certified' to conduct these assessments and interpret their results for leaders. If leadership development is largely focused on personality awareness, that makes those experts hugely valuable and powerful.

The ability to conduct and interpret the findings of these assessments is only a part of their allure. The real juice comes from holding informational power over leaders with much more seniority, status, and influence than most talent professionals.

For a brief time during the assessment process, the most senior leaders in the organization become subordinate to those who know 'who they really are,' including their special leadership sauce and their derailers. This feeds the ego and self-importance of professionals who are too often overlooked.

Who recommends or decides what leadership programs the organization will invest in to make their leaders better? The same professionals whose sense of value and importance comes from selecting the assessment approach. Exposing the self-interest in a popular approach is not easy to hear, but it is undeniable.
